title: Sequence-length-aware slot packing and slow-start admission playbook for hosted GPU stability
creator: Liam O'Connor
description: Post-incident follow-up for a hosted GPU capacity exhaustion event where a small fraction of very long-sequence requests amplified queue length and prevented autoscaler prewarm from stabilizing pools. This ticket scopes an engineering playbook to add sequence-length-aware slot packing plus a slow-start (probe) admission path to reduce queue amplification, improve fairness, and avoid oscillatory scaling behavior.
steps_taken: 2025-03-01 03:14 UTC - Detection: alerted by queue-depth and tail-latency dashboards (gpu-pools.prod).
2025-03-01 03:22 UTC - Emergency mitigation: applied short-term tenant-level soft cap on sequences > 16k tokens via rate limiter; bumped pool autoscaler min-replicas by +2 for affected region.
2025-03-01 04:10 UTC - Traffic steering: rerouted low-priority requests to lower-cost pool and enabled temporary overflow fallback to dedicated capacity for a subset of heavy tenants.

2025-03-02 - Data collection: enabled high-fidelity tracing for sequence_length, KV-cache hit ratio, per-request memory delta, and actual GPU utilization; exported traces to capacity-incident S3 bundle for analysis.
2025-03-03 - Interim mitigations reviewed with SRE and PM: preserve soft caps and add probe admission for suspect tenants during peak windows.
findings: Root cause: skewed request distribution - ~1.8% of requests had sequences > 12k tokens and consumed disproportionately large KV cache/memory for long durations, blocking slot reuse.
Autoscaler reactions were delayed because pod-level memory metrics underreported transient KV-cache pressure; scheduler kept fewer pods online than needed during the surge window.
Existing slot-packing ignored sequence length; packing long sequences with short ones caused long tail latencies and queue buildup for short requests (head-of-line blocking).
KV-cache contention reduced effective throughput per GPU; naive prewarm/priming failed because new pods required several large-sequence requests to fill KV cache before reaching steady throughput.

Observed oscillation: prewarm triggered, long requests flooded primed pods, causing evictions of short-request traffic and autoscaler to scale up; when surge subsided, scale-down was aggressive, leading to repeated cycles.
decisions: Implement sequence-length-aware slot packing in the admission layer: group requests with similar max_seq windows and cap slot lifetimes to limit head-of-line blocking.

Introduce a slow-start admission path for long-sequence clients: gentle probing (1-2 requests) to prime KV cache and only allow higher concurrency after successful probes within latency and memory bounds.
Adjust autoscaler to track transient KV-cache memory signals (application-level metric) and use a conservative downscale window for pools that recently experienced long-sequence ramps.
Rollout changes behind a feature flag with progressive canary by tenant and region; include telemetry hooks before enabling global rollout.

notes: Trade-offs considered: blocking long sequences at the API layer impacts latency for those customers; slow-start probe balances customer experience vs platform stability.

We considered forcing early down-sampling/summary for extremely long inputs (model-side truncation) but decided that platform-level admission plus tenant opt-in trimming is less risky for correctness.
Plan to coordinate tenant communications for customers affected by soft caps and to offer dedicated capacity guidance where appropriate.
